# Binaural Synthesis Method Using Multiple Physical Sound Sources

## Overview

This method describes an approach to operating a first device equipped with a plurality of physical sound sources—specifically at least four—arranged to enable accurate binaural synthesis of at least one virtual sound source. By strategically positioning multiple acoustic transducers relative to each ear, the method achieves realistic spatial audio reproduction that leverages the natural acoustic filtering properties of the human ear.

## Device Configuration and Physical Sound Source Placement

The device is configured such that when worn by a user, at least two physical sound sources are positioned in closer proximity to the first ear than to the second ear, while a corresponding set of at least two physical sound sources are positioned closer to the second ear than to the first ear. This dual-sided arrangement, employing no fewer than four physical sound sources in total (a minimum of two per ear), establishes the foundational architecture necessary for sophisticated binaural audio rendering.

This configuration is deliberately designed to exploit the acoustic properties of the pinna—the visible, outer part of the human ear. For each ear, at least two of the physical sound sources are specifically arranged to acoustically induce natural directional pinna cues. These cues correspond to different directions of sound arrival, meaning that the varied positioning of the sound sources relative to each ear naturally recreates the spectral filtering effects that the pinna would produce when sound arrives from different directions in real-world listening conditions. This approach allows the device to leverage the user's own anatomical acoustic filtering, rather than relying solely on artificial or generalized processing algorithms, to convey directional information.

## Audio Signal Processing

The method further encompasses a signal processing stage in which the device receives at least one audio input signal. This input signal undergoes processing to generate a processed version of the signal, which is then prepared for distribution across the various physical sound sources positioned around each ear. The processing stage is instrumental in shaping the signal so that, when reproduced through the multiple physical sound sources, it contributes to the perception of a virtual sound source positioned at a desired spatial location.

## Frequency-Dependent Signal Distribution

A key aspect of this method involves the distribution of the processed audio signal across the at least two physical sound sources associated with each ear, specifically within a frequency range spanning at least 4 kHz to 12 kHz. This frequency range is particularly significant because it encompasses the spectral region where pinna-induced spectral cues are most perceptually relevant for human sound localization, particularly for discerning elevation and front-back disambiguation.

By distributing the processed signal across multiple physical sound sources within this critical frequency band, the method ensures that the natural directional cues induced by the pinna are effectively reinforced and utilized. This targeted frequency distribution, combined with the strategic physical positioning of the sound sources, allows the device to synthesize a convincing binaural experience wherein the user perceives a virtual sound source as originating from a specific, realistic location in space—despite the sound being generated by discrete physical transducers integrated into the device.

## Conclusion

This method represents a sophisticated approach to binaural audio synthesis that combines careful physical transducer placement with targeted signal processing and frequency-specific distribution. By leveraging natural pinna cues through the arrangement of multiple physical sound sources per ear, and by focusing signal distribution on the perceptually critical 4 kHz to 12 kHz frequency range, the method enables more accurate and natural virtual sound source localization than approaches relying on a single sound source per ear or purely synthetic spatial processing techniques.

# Method for Binaural Synthesis Using Multiple Physical Sound Sources with Natural Pinna Cue Induction

## Overview

This method addresses a persistent challenge in binaural audio synthesis: the accurate and reliable reproduction of virtual sound sources that are perceived by a listener as originating from specific, natural-sounding directions in space. Traditional approaches to binaural synthesis have relied heavily on digital signal processing techniques—particularly Head-Related Transfer Function (HRTF) filtering—to artificially impart directional cues onto an audio signal before delivering it to the listener's ears, typically via headphones. While these techniques have achieved considerable success, they suffer from well-documented limitations, including front-back confusion, elevation perception errors, in-head localization, and significant listener-to-listener variability due to the highly individualized nature of pinna (outer ear) morphology and its effect on sound diffraction and reflection.

The present method takes a fundamentally different approach by leveraging the listener's own pinna as a natural, physical filter, rather than attempting to digitally simulate its effects.

## Core Structural Configuration

The method operates through a device incorporating **at least four physical sound sources** (such as miniature transducers, speakers, or drivers), which are deliberately and precisely positioned relative to the listener's ears. The critical design constraint is that these sound sources are arranged such that, **for each individual ear**, at least two of the physical sound sources are positioned to acoustically interact with the pinna from different spatial angles or directions.

This positioning is not arbitrary. It is specifically engineered so that the sound emitted from each of these at least two sources, per ear, undergoes natural acoustic interaction with the folds, ridges, and cavities of the pinna—interactions that include diffraction, reflection, and resonance effects that are characteristic of how sound naturally arrives at the ear from different directions in real-world listening environments. Because each source is positioned at a distinct angle relative to the ear, the pinna imparts genuinely different, direction-specific spectral modifications to the sound emitted by each source. These modifications are the same type of natural acoustic cues that the human auditory system has evolved to interpret as indicators of sound source direction and elevation.

## Signal Processing and Distribution

The method further comprises specific signal processing steps applied to an incoming audio input signal—representing the sound of the virtual source to be synthesized. This audio input signal is:

1. **Received and analyzed** to determine the desired virtual spatial position of the sound source.
2. **Processed and distributed** across the at least two physical sound sources associated with each ear, according to a distribution scheme designed to control the relative contribution of each source.
3. **Frequency-band specific**, in that this distribution and processing is particularly applied within the frequency range of **4 kHz to 12 kHz**—a range recognized in psychoacoustic research as being especially critical for pinna-based directional and elevation cues, as it corresponds to wavelengths comparable to the physical dimensions of the pinna's structures.

By controlling the relative amplitude, phase, or timing of the signal delivered to each of the at least two sources per ear within this frequency band, the method effectively allows the natural pinna filtering effects associated with each source's distinct position to be blended, weighted, or emphasized. This enables the perceived direction of the virtual source to be synthesized or "steered" between the actual physical positions of the real sound sources, using genuine acoustic cues rather than mathematically modeled ones.

## Advantages and Rationale

The central advantage of this approach lies in its use of **authentic, listener-specific pinna interactions** rather than generic or averaged HRTF models. Conventional HRTF-based binaural synthesis typically relies on filters derived from measurements taken from a standardized mannequin (such as a KEMAR head) or from a limited set of individual measurements, which may not accurately reflect the unique pinna geometry of the actual listener. This mismatch between the applied filter and the listener's own anatomy is a well-known source of localization errors and perceptual artifacts, including the sensation that sounds originate from inside the head rather than from an external, spatially defined position.

By contrast, because this method uses the listener's own physical pinna to naturally filter and shape the sound in real time, the directional cues produced are inherently and automatically matched to that specific listener's anatomy. There is no need to measure, model, or approximate the listener's HRTF in advance. The pinna performs its natural acoustic function exactly as it would for a real, physically located sound source, resulting in cues that are inherently authentic and individually accurate.

## Resulting Benefits

This approach yields several practical improvements over conventional binaural synthesis techniques:

- **Enhanced Realism**: Because the directional cues are physically genuine rather than digitally simulated, the perceived spatial position of the virtual sound source tends to be more natural, convincing, and stable.
- **Reduced Localization Errors**: The reliance on real pinna interaction helps mitigate common issues such as front-back confusion and elevation ambiguity, which frequently arise from imperfect HRTF modeling.
- **Listener Independence**: Since the method does not depend on a pre-measured or modeled HRTF specific to an individual, it can generalize more effectively across different listeners without requiring personalized calibration.
- **Improved Robustness**: The combination of multiple physical sources with targeted frequency-band processing provides a flexible and reliable framework for synthesizing a range of virtual source positions with consistent perceptual quality.

In summary, this method reimagines binaural synthesis by shifting the burden of directional cue generation from artificial digital filtering to genuine physical acoustics, using a carefully arranged multi-source device and targeted frequency-specific signal processing to achieve more natural, accurate, and reliable spatial audio perception.

# Patent Claim Draft

## Claim 1

A method for binaural audio synthesis using a wearable device, the method comprising:

providing a wearable device configured to be worn on or around a user's head, the wearable device comprising, for each ear of the user, a plurality of physical sound-emitting transducers positioned at a corresponding plurality of distinct locations relative to a pinna of the ear, wherein the distinct locations are selected such that acoustic radiation from each transducer interacts differently with anatomical features of the pinna to naturally induce spectral cues associated with sound source elevation and front-back disambiguation;

receiving an input audio signal and spatial metadata indicative of a desired virtual sound source position relative to the user's head, the desired virtual sound source position defined at least by an azimuth angle and an elevation angle;

determining, based on the spatial metadata, a set of transducer drive signals for the plurality of physical sound-emitting transducers of at least one ear, wherein determining the set of transducer drive signals comprises computing a gain and/or delay value for each transducer of the plurality based on a mapping between the desired virtual sound source position and the distinct physical locations of the transducers relative to the pinna, such that a combination of acoustic outputs from the plurality of transducers, as naturally filtered by the pinna, produces a perceived spatial cue at the user's eardrum corresponding to the desired elevation angle without applying a synthetic head-related transfer function elevation filter to the input audio signal; and

driving the plurality of physical sound-emitting transducers of the at least one ear according to the determined set of transducer drive signals to render the input audio signal such that the user perceives the virtual sound source at the desired azimuth angle and elevation angle.

---

## Dependent Claims (illustrative)

**Claim 2.** The method of claim 1, wherein the plurality of physical sound-emitting transducers for each ear comprises at least three transducers positioned respectively proximate to a cymba conchae region, a cavum conchae region, and a helix region of the pinna.

**Claim 3.** The method of claim 1, wherein determining the set of transducer drive signals comprises interpolating between a plurality of pre-stored gain/delay coefficient sets, each pre-stored coefficient set associated with a predetermined virtual source position, to compute the gain and/or delay value for a virtual source position falling between the predetermined virtual source positions.

**Claim 4.** The method of claim 1, further comprising applying, to the input audio signal prior to determining the set of transducer drive signals, an interaural time difference and/or interaural level difference corresponding to the azimuth angle of the desired virtual sound source position, wherein the interaural time difference and/or interaural level difference is applied between the transducer drive signals of a first ear and transducer drive signals of a second ear.

**Claim 5.** The method of claim 1, wherein the mapping between the desired virtual sound source position and the distinct physical locations of the transducers is derived from a calibration process comprising measuring, for the user or for a representative population of users, acoustic transfer functions from each of the plurality of transducer locations to a microphone positioned at or near an eardrum position.

**Claim 6.** The method of claim 1, wherein the wearable device is an open-ear or ear-adjacent device that does not occlude an ear canal entrance, such that the plurality of physical sound-emitting transducers radiate sound into the pinna without direct insertion into the ear canal.

**Claim 7.** The method of claim 1, wherein computing the gain and/or delay value for each transducer further comprises applying a distance-dependent scaling factor derived from the spatial metadata to synthesize a perceived distance of the virtual sound source.

**Claim 8.** The method of claim 1, further comprising dynamically updating the set of transducer drive signals in response to a detected change in orientation of the user's head, the detected change being received from a head-tracking sensor integrated with or communicatively coupled to the wearable device.

**Claim 9.** The method of claim 1, wherein the plurality of physical sound-emitting transducers comprises micro-speakers, and wherein at least two of the micro-speakers are angled at different orientations relative to a plane of the pinna to produce direction-dependent diffraction and reflection cues.

**Claim 10.** A wearable audio device configured to perform the method of claim 1, the wearable audio device comprising: the plurality of physical sound-emitting transducers for each ear; a processor; and a non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by the processor, cause the wearable audio device to perform the method of claim 1.

# CLAIM AND SPECIFICATION LANGUAGE FOR MULTI-SPEAKER DIRECTIONAL AUDIO REPRODUCTION SYSTEM

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to audio reproduction systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus for reproducing directional sound cues to a user through a plurality of speakers arranged in spatial relation to the user's ears, thereby enabling perception of sound source localization corresponding to a virtual or captured acoustic environment.

---

## BACKGROUND

Conventional stereo and binaural audio reproduction systems often fail to provide accurate perception of sound source direction, particularly with respect to elevation and front-back disambiguation. There exists a need for an apparatus and method capable of reproducing directional audio cues with improved spatial fidelity through the use of multiple discrete transducers positioned about the user's auditory periphery.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with one or more embodiments, there is provided a system and method for reproducing directional sound cues to a user by way of at least four speakers arranged about the user's ears, wherein each speaker is configured to emit an audio signal derived from a source audio stream, the audio signal being modified according to at least one directional parameter corresponding to a desired perceived location of a virtual sound source relative to the user.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF EXEMPLARY EMBODIMENTS

### System Architecture

In one embodiment, the directional audio reproduction system comprises a speaker arrangement including a first speaker, a second speaker, a third speaker, and a fourth speaker (collectively, "the plurality of speakers"), each of the plurality of speakers being positioned at a predetermined location relative to a user's head, such that the plurality of speakers substantially surrounds at least one ear of the user.

In certain embodiments, the first speaker may be disposed forward of the user's ear, the second speaker may be disposed rearward of the user's ear, the third speaker may be disposed above the user's ear, and the fourth speaker may be disposed below the user's ear, such that the plurality of speakers defines a spatial array about the user's ear in at least two orthogonal planes.

It will be appreciated that the number, arrangement, and relative positioning of the speakers may be varied without departing from the scope of the present disclosure, and that additional speakers may be incorporated to further enhance directional resolution.

### Processing Module

The system further comprises a processing module operatively coupled to the plurality of speakers, the processing module being configured to:

(a) receive a source audio signal representative of a sound to be reproduced;

(b) obtain directional data indicative of a desired perceived spatial location of a virtual sound source relative to the user, the directional data comprising at least one of an azimuth value, an elevation value, and a distance value;

(c) generate, based at least in part on the directional data, a plurality of speaker-specific audio signals, each speaker-specific audio signal corresponding to one of the plurality of speakers; and

(d) transmit each speaker-specific audio signal to its corresponding speaker for reproduction thereof.

In some embodiments, the generation of the plurality of speaker-specific audio signals comprises applying at least one of a gain adjustment, a phase adjustment, a time delay, and a frequency-dependent filtering operation to the source audio signal, wherein the gain adjustment, phase adjustment, time delay, or frequency-dependent filtering operation applied to a given speaker-specific audio signal is determined as a function of the directional data and a relative position of the corresponding speaker with respect to the desired perceived spatial location of the virtual sound source.

### Directional Cue Synthesis

In accordance with certain embodiments, the processing module is further configured to apply a head-related transfer function (HRTF), or an approximation thereof, to the source audio signal in generating the plurality of speaker-specific audio signals, wherein the head-related transfer function is selected or computed based at least in part on the directional data and, optionally, one or more anatomical parameters associated with the user.

In further embodiments, the processing module may be configured to dynamically update the plurality of speaker-specific audio signals in response to a change in the directional data, a change in an orientation of the user's head, or a change in a position of the user, such change being detected by way of at least one sensor operatively coupled to the processing module, the at least one sensor comprising, for example, an inertial measurement unit, a gyroscope, an accelerometer, a magnetometer, or a camera-based tracking system.

### Exemplary Method

In one embodiment, a method for reproducing directional sound cues to a user is provided, the method comprising:

positioning at least four speakers about at least one ear of the user, such that a first speaker and a second speaker are positioned along a first axis relative to the ear, and a third speaker and a fourth speaker are positioned along a second axis relative to the ear, the second axis being non-parallel to the first axis;

receiving a source audio signal;

determining directional data corresponding to a desired perceived location of a virtual sound source;

generating a plurality of speaker-specific signals from the source audio signal based on the directional data and respective positions of the at least four speakers; and

driving the at least four speakers with the respective speaker-specific signals so as to produce, at the at least one ear of the user, a composite acoustic signal perceptually corresponding to the desired perceived location of the virtual sound source.

---

## EXEMPLARY CLAIMS

**Claim 1.** A system for reproducing directional sound cues to a user, the system comprising:

at least four speakers configured to be arranged about at least one ear of the user;

a processing module operatively coupled to the at least four speakers, the processing module being configured to:

receive a source audio signal;

obtain directional data indicative of a desired perceived spatial location of a virtual sound source relative to the user;

generate, based on the directional data, a plurality of speaker-specific audio signals respectively corresponding to the at least four speakers; and

cause the at least four speakers to emit the respective speaker-specific audio signals so as to produce a composite acoustic output perceptible by the user as originating from the desired perceived spatial location.

**Claim 2.** The system of claim 1, wherein the at least four speakers comprise a first speaker positioned forward of the user's ear, a second speaker positioned rearward of the user's ear, a third speaker positioned above the user's ear, and a fourth speaker positioned below the user's ear.

**Claim 3.** The system of claim 1, wherein generating the plurality of speaker-specific audio signals comprises applying a head-related transfer function to the source audio signal.

**Claim 4.** The system of claim 1, further comprising at least one sensor configured to detect an orientation of the user's head, wherein the processing module is further configured to update the plurality of speaker-specific audio signals based on the detected orientation.

**Claim 5.** The system of claim 1, wherein generating the plurality of speaker-specific audio signals comprises applying at least one of a gain adjustment, a time delay, and a frequency-dependent filter to the source audio signal, the gain adjustment, time delay, or frequency-dependent filter being determined based on a relative position between a respective speaker and the desired perceived spatial location of the virtual sound source.

**Claim 6.** A method for reproducing directional sound cues, comprising the steps substantially as described in the specification hereinabove.

---

*It will be understood by those skilled in the art that the foregoing embodiments are exemplary in nature and that various modifications, additions, and alternative configurations may be made without departing from the scope and spirit of the present disclosure, as defined by the appended claims.*

# PATENT APPLICATION

## TITLE OF INVENTION
**AUDIO DEVICE WITH MULTIPLE TRANSDUCERS FOR SIMULATING NATURAL DIRECTIONAL HEARING CUES**

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to audio reproduction devices, and more particularly to head-worn or head-mounted audio devices employing a plurality of spatially distributed transducers configured to reproduce natural interaural time differences, interaural level differences, and spectral cues associated with directional human hearing.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Conventional headphones and earphones typically employ a single transducer per ear positioned in close proximity to the ear canal. While such configurations are effective for reproducing basic stereo audio content, they suffer from significant limitations with respect to spatial audio perception. Specifically, single-transducer-per-ear designs fail to reproduce the complex acoustic cues that the human auditory system relies upon to localize sound sources in three-dimensional space.

Natural human sound localization depends on a combination of cues, including:

1. **Interaural Time Differences (ITD)** — the difference in arrival time of a sound wave at each ear, primarily useful for localizing lower-frequency sounds;
2. **Interaural Level Differences (ILD)** — the difference in sound pressure level between the two ears, caused by head shadowing effects, primarily useful for higher-frequency sounds;
3. **Spectral Cues** — frequency-dependent filtering effects imparted by the pinna (outer ear), head, and torso, which assist in resolving front-back and up-down ambiguities, collectively described by the Head-Related Transfer Function (HRTF).

Attempts to simulate spatial audio using conventional two-transducer headphone systems typically rely entirely on digital signal processing (DSP)-based HRTF convolution. While such approaches can be effective, they are computationally intensive, require accurate HRTF measurements tailored to individual users (as HRTFs vary significantly between individuals due to differences in pinna shape, head size, and torso geometry), and often produce artifacts such as front-back confusion, in-head localization, or coloration artifacts when the HRTF does not closely match the listener's own anatomy.

There exists a need for an audio device that physically reproduces directional acoustic cues through the spatial arrangement of multiple transducers, thereby reducing reliance on computationally intensive and listener-specific DSP-based HRTF simulation, while improving the naturalness and accuracy of perceived sound source localization.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention provides an audio device comprising at least four transducers arranged in a spatially distributed configuration about the head of a user, such that each ear of the user receives sound energy from multiple transducers positioned at different locations relative to the head. This arrangement enables the device to physically recreate, at least in part, the natural time-of-arrival differences, level differences, and spectral filtering effects that occur in natural, unamplified hearing, rather than relying solely on digital emulation of such effects.

In one embodiment, the audio device comprises a head-worn support structure (such as a headband, eyeglass frame, neckband, or helmet-integrated structure) supporting at least four transducers, with at least two transducers associated with each ear of the user. The transducers associated with a given ear are positioned at different locations relative to that ear — for example, one transducer positioned forward of the ear, and another positioned rearward of the ear — such that sound arriving at the ear (or at a microphone/ear-canal-reference-point associated with the ear) from each transducer arrives with a distinct time delay, level, and spectral coloration relative to the other transducer(s) associated with that ear.

By controlling the relative timing, amplitude, and frequency content of the signals delivered to each of the at least four transducers via an associated signal processing unit, the device can synthesize a wide range of perceived source directions and distances with improved naturalness and reduced computational burden relative to conventional single-transducer-per-ear HRTF-convolution approaches, while also permitting partial physical reproduction of pinna-interaction effects when transducers are positioned to direct sound into the concha and pinna structures from varying angles.

---

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

**FIG. 1** is a top plan view of a user's head illustrating the general placement of four transducers in accordance with one embodiment of the invention.

**FIG. 2** is a perspective view of a head-worn support structure incorporating four transducers in a headband-style configuration.

**FIG. 3** is a schematic block diagram illustrating the signal processing architecture used to drive the plurality of transducers.

**FIG. 4** is a side view of a single ear region illustrating the angular and distance relationship between a forward transducer and a rearward transducer relative to the ear canal entrance.

**FIG. 5** is a flow diagram illustrating a method of processing an input audio signal into a plurality of transducer-specific drive signals based on a desired virtual sound source location.

**FIG. 6** illustrates an alternative embodiment employing six transducers, including transducers positioned above and below the ear.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### General Overview

Referring to FIG. 1, there is shown a top plan view of a user's head 100 having a left ear 102 and a right ear 104. In accordance with the present invention, an audio device 110 comprises at least four transducers: a first transducer 112 and a second transducer 114 associated with the left ear 102, and a third transducer 116 and a fourth transducer 118 associated with the right ear 104.

The first transducer 112 is positioned generally forward of the left ear 102, while the second transducer 114 is positioned generally rearward of the left ear 102. Similarly, the third transducer 116 is positioned generally forward of the right ear 104, and the fourth transducer 118 is positioned generally rearward of the right ear 104. In alternative embodiments, transducers may additionally or alternatively be positioned above, below, or at other angular positions relative to each ear, as discussed further below with respect to FIG. 6.

Each transducer 112, 114, 116, 118 is preferably a miniature electroacoustic transducer, including but not limited to a dynamic (moving-coil) driver, balanced-armature driver, planar-magnetic driver, piezoelectric transducer, or MEMS-based microspeaker. # Spatial Audio Reproduction System Utilizing Multiple Per-Ear Transducers for Virtual Directional Synthesis

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to audio signal processing and electroacoustic transducer systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus for synthesizing perceived directionality of virtual sound sources through the coordinated frequency-dependent distribution of audio signals across a plurality of physically discrete transducers positioned proximate to each ear of a listener.

---

## Background of the Invention

Conventional binaural and stereophonic reproduction systems typically employ a single transducer per ear (e.g., in headphone or earbud form factors) to convey directional audio cues through interaural time differences (ITD), interaural level differences (ILD), and head-related transfer function (HRTF) filtering applied via digital signal processing. While such systems can simulate externalized sound sources through convolution with HRTF datasets, they are inherently limited in their ability to reproduce fine-grained spectral cues associated with pinna filtering, elevation perception, and front-back disambiguation, particularly when relying on generic (non-individualized) HRTF models.

Multi-driver headphone systems exist in the prior art primarily for the purpose of frequency-range division among drivers optimized for bass, midrange, and treble reproduction (analogous to loudspeaker crossover architectures). However, such systems do not utilize the spatial arrangement of multiple drivers per ear as a mechanism for directional synthesis; rather, driver placement in such systems is dictated by acoustic and mechanical design considerations unrelated to spatial perception.

There exists a need for a reproduction system that leverages the physical positioning of multiple discrete acoustic sources per ear, in combination with frequency-specific signal routing, to synthesize virtual source directionality with improved perceptual accuracy, reduced reliance on generic HRTF convolution, and enhanced externalization.

---

## Summary of the Invention

The invention provides a spatial audio reproduction apparatus and associated signal processing method comprising:

1. A plurality of physically discrete acoustic transducers ("sub-sources") disposed at distinct spatial positions relative to each ear of a listener, each sub-source being mechanically coupled to a support structure (e.g., an earcup, earpiece shell, or open-ear frame) such that the sub-sources maintain fixed or adjustable geometric relationships to the pinna and ear canal entrance;

2. A signal decomposition module configured to divide an input audio signal, corresponding to a virtual sound source having an intended direction and/or distance, into a plurality of frequency-band-specific sub-signals;

3. A spatial mapping module configured to assign each frequency-band-specific sub-signal to one or more of the plurality of sub-sources per ear, based on a correspondence between (a) the frequency content of the sub-signal, (b) the physical position of each sub-source relative to the ear, and (c) the intended virtual direction of the source, such that the combined acoustic output of the sub-sources reconstructs, at the entrance of the ear canal, an interaural and monaural cue set approximating that which would be produced by an actual sound source at the intended virtual position;

4. A dynamic weighting and crossfading unit configured to adjust, in real time, the relative gain and phase of each sub-source's contribution as the intended virtual direction changes, thereby synthesizing continuous or quantized virtual source movement (panning) across the sub-source array; and

5. Optionally, a head-tracking input and individualized calibration subsystem configured to adjust the frequency-to-sub-source mapping in dependence on measured or estimated pinna geometry and head orientation.

---

## Detailed Description

### 1. Physical Transducer Arrangement

In a preferred embodiment, each ear is served by a plurality of sub-sources (N ≥ 2, typically 3–8) arranged at distinct positions including, without limitation:

- **Anterior (front-facing) position**, directed toward the concha and tragus;
- **Posterior (rear-facing) position**, directed toward the posterior pinna wall;
- **Superior (top-facing) position**, directed toward the helix/upper concha region;
- **Inferior (bottom-facing) position**, directed toward the lobule region;
- **Central/axial position**, directed axially into the ear canal entrance (conventional driver placement).

Each sub-source may comprise a moving-coil dynamic driver, balanced-armature driver, piezoelectric transducer, or micro-electrostatic element, selected according to the frequency range to be reproduced by that sub-source. Sub-sources may be mechanically isolated from one another via acoustic damping structures to minimize unintended cross-coupling and comb-filtering artifacts.

The physical separation between sub-sources, though small in absolute terms (on the order of 5–30 mm), is sufficient—particularly at higher frequencies where wavelengths become comparable to or smaller than such separations—to produce measurably distinct spectral and level cues at the ear canal entrance as a function of which sub-source(s) are active. This physical diversity is exploited, rather than relying solely on digital HRTF filtering, to produce directional cues.

### 2. Frequency-Specific Signal Distribution

A central and inventive aspect of the system is the **frequency-dependent distribution** of the input signal among the sub-sources, governed by the following principles:

**(a) Low-frequency signals** (e.g., below approximately 500 Hz), for which interaural cues are dominated by ITD and for which the wavelength is large relative to sub-source spacing, are substantially reproduced by all sub-sources in a summed, phase-coherent manner, or predominantly by a central sub-source, since directional discrimination at these frequencies is not significantly affected by sub-source position.

**(b) Mid-frequency signals** (e.g., approximately 500 Hz–3 kHz), for which ILD and early pinna reflections begin to contribute to localization, are distributed among two or more sub-sources with a gain distribution computed as a function of the intended virtual azimuth and/or elevation angle, according to a stored or computed transfer function set correlating sub-source position to equivalent free-field source angle.

**(c) High-frequency signals** (e.g., above approximately 3 kHz), which are primarily responsible for elevation perception and front-back disambiguation via pinna spectral filtering, are selectively routed to the sub-source(s) whose physical position most closely replicates the spectral notch/peak pattern that the pinna would naturally impose on a sound arriving from the intended virtual direction. For example:

- A virtual source intended to be perceived as originating from above and behind the listener preferentially activates the superior-posterior sub-source(s), whose direct acoustic path to the ear canal, combined with the natural pinna geometry, replicates the spectral signature of an elevated rear source;
- A virtual source intended to be perceived as originating from directly in front activates the anterior sub-source(s) with minimal high-frequency energy routed to posterior sub-sources, reducing front-back confusion.

This frequency-specific routing may be implemented via a bank of digital crossover filters (e.g., linear-phase FIR filters or minimum-phase IIR filters) whose cutoff frequencies, slopes, and per-band gain coefficients are determined by a **direction-to-distribution mapping function**, which may be:

- A parametric function derived from anthropometric averages;
- A lookup table populated from individualized or generic HRTF magnitude data, decomposed into per-sub-source contributions via an optimization process (e.g., least-squares fitting or spectral matching) that solves for the gain vector **g**(f, θ, φ) across sub-sources that best reproduces the target HRTF magnitude and phase response at each frequency band, for azimuth θ and elevation φ;
- Adaptively updated based on calibration measurements taken via in-ear microphones during a setup routine.

### 3. Signal Processing Chain

The processing chain, executed on a digital signal processor (DSP), application processor, or dedicated ASIC, comprises:

1. **Input stage**: Receipt of a monophonic, stereophonic, or object-based audio signal, together with associated metadata specifying intended virtual source position(s), which may be static or time-varying (e.g., for moving virtual sources or in conjunction with head-tracking data);

2. **Analysis stage**: Time-frequency decomposition of the input signal (e.g., via STFT, QMF filterbank, or wavelet decomposition) into a plurality of frequency bands;

3. **Mapping stage**: For each frequency band and each ear, retrieval or computation of a gain (and optionally phase/delay) coefficient for each sub-source, based on the direction-to-distribution mapping function and the current intended virtual direction;

4. **Synthesis stage**: Application of the computed coefficients to the corresponding frequency-band signal components, followed by reconstruction (e.g., inverse STFT) of a discrete time-domain drive signal for each individual sub-source;

5. **Output stage**: Delivery of the per-sub-source drive signals to the corresponding transducers, with optional per-channel equalization to compensate for individual transducer response and mechanical/acoustic coupling effects.

### 4. Dynamic Panning and Crossfading

To synthesize continuous virtual source movement, the weighting coefficients applied to each sub-source are updated at a control rate sufficient to avoid perceptible artifacts (e.g., 100 Hz–1 kHz update rate), with interpolation (e.g., linear, cosine, or spherical interpolation across the direction-to-distribution mapping function) applied between discrete calibration or lookup-table points to produce smooth panning trajectories across the sub-source array, analogous to vector-based amplitude panning (VBAP) techniques employed in loudspeaker arrays, but adapted to the near-field, sub-wavelength geometry of a per-ear transducer cluster and incorporating frequency-dependent divergence in the panning law as described above.

### 5. Calibration and Personalization

In certain embodiments, the apparatus further comprises:

- One or more **in-ear or ear-canal-entrance microphones** configured to capture the combined acoustic output of the sub-source array during a calibration sequence in which test signals (e.g., swept sinusoids, maximum length sequences) are played from each sub-source individually and in combination;
- A **calibration processor** configured to compare the measured response against a target HRTF or target spectral cue set (which may be generic, anthropometrically estimated, or individually measured via prior free-field measurement) and to compute or refine the direction-to-distribution mapping function accordingly, on a per-user basis;
- A **head-tracking sensor** (e.g., inertial measurement unit) configured to provide real-time head orientation data, used to adjust the intended virtual direction relative to the listener's instantaneous head pose, such that virtual sources maintain a stable perceived position in world-fixed (rather than head-fixed) coordinates.

---

## Illustrative Claims (Non-Limiting Examples)

1. An audio reproduction apparatus comprising: a plurality of acoustic transducers disposed at mutually distinct positions relative to a single ear of a listener; a signal processor configured to decompose an input audio signal associated with a virtual sound source direction into a plurality of frequency bands; and a mapping module configured to assign, to each of the plurality of transducers, a frequency-band-dependent gain coefficient determined at least in part by the physical position of the respective transducer relative to the ear and by the virtual sound source direction, such that the combined output of the plurality of transducers synthesizes, at the ear canal entrance, spectral and level cues corresponding to the virtual sound source direction.

2. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the plurality of transducers comprises at least one transducer directed toward an anterior region of the pinna and at least one transducer directed toward a posterior region of the pinna, and wherein high-frequency signal content above a threshold frequency is distributed between said transducers in dependence on an azimuthal component of the virtual sound source direction.
